source_text: Venio itaque ad illum articulum quem et nostri praetendunt ad ineundam curiositatem et haeretici inculcant ad importandam scrupulositatem. Scriptum est, inquiunt, Quaerite, et invenietis. Quando hanc vocem dominus emisit, recordemur. Puto in primitiis ipsis doctrinae suae, cum adhuc dubitaretur apud omnes, an Christus esset, et cum adhuc nec Petrus illum dei filium pronuntiasset, cum etiam Ioannes de illo certus esse desisset. Merito ergo tunc dictum est, Quaerite et invenietis, quando quaerendus adhuc erat qui adhuc agnitus non erat. Et hoc quantum ad Iudaeos. Ad illos enim pertinet totus sermo suggillationis istius, qui habebant ubi quaererent Christum. Habent, inquit, Moysen et Heliam, id est legem et prophetas Christum praedicantes, secundum quod alibi aperte: Scrutamini scripturas, in quibus salutem speratis; illae enim de me loquuntur. Hoc erit, Quaerite et invenietis. Nam et sequentia in Iudaeos competere manifestum est, Pulsate et aperietur vobis. Iudaei retro penes deum fuerant, dehinc eiecti ob delicta extra deum esse coeperunt. Nationes vero nunquam penes deum, nisi stillicidium de situla et pulvis ex area et foris semper. Ita qui foris semper, quomodo pulsabit eo ubi nunquam fuit? quam ianuam novit, in qua nec receptus nec eiectus aliquando? an qui scit se intus fuisse et foras actum, is potius pulsavit, et ostium novit? Etiam, Petite et accipietis, ei competit qui sciebat a quo esset petendum, a quo et erat aliquid repromissum, a deo scilicet Abraham, Isaac et Iacob, quem nationes non magis noverant quam ullam repromissionem eius. Et ideo ad IsraÃ«l loquebatur: Non sum, inquit, missus, nisi ad oves perditas domus IsraÃ«l. Nondum canibus iactarat panem filiorum, nondum in viam nationum ire mandabat. Siquidem in fine praecipit, vaderent ad docendas et tinguendas nationes, consecuturi mox spiritum sanctum paracletum, qui illos deducturus esset in omnem veritatem. Et hoc ergo illo facit. Quodsi nationibus destinati doctores apostoli, ipsi quoque doctorem consecuturi erant paracletum, multo magis vacabat erga nos, Quaerite et invenietis, quibus ultro erat obventura doctrina per apostolos et ipsis apostolis per spiritum sanctum. Omnia quidem domini dicta omnibus posita sunt; per aures Iudaeorum ad nos transierunt. Sed pleraque in personas directa non proprietatem admonitionis nobis constituerunt, sed exemplum.
thought_title: The command to seek was for the Jews before Christ was known
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the gospel command 'Seek and you will find' was addressed to the Jews before they recognized Christ, not to Christians who already believe.
pass_a_gloss: I come therefore to that point which both our people put forward for entering upon curiosity and the heretics press in for bringing in scrupulosity. It is written, they say, Seek, and you will find. Let us remember when the Lord uttered this saying. I think in the very first beginnings of his teaching, when it was still being doubted among all whether he was the Christ, and when not yet even Peter had declared him the son of God, when also John had ceased to be certain about him. Rightly therefore was it said then, Seek and you will find, when he was still to be sought who had not yet been recognized. And this as far as the Jews. For to them belongs the whole discourse of that reproof, who had where to seek Christ. They have, he says, Moses and Elijah, that is the law and the prophets preaching Christ, according to which elsewhere openly: Search the Scriptures, in which you hope for salvation; for they speak about me. This will be, Seek and you will find. For also the following things are manifest to apply to the Jews: Knock and it will be opened to you. The Jews formerly had been with God, thereafter cast out because of offenses they began to be outside God. The nations however never with God, except a drop from a bucket and dust from a threshing floor and always outside. Thus he who is always outside, how will he knock where he never was? What door does he know, in which he was neither received nor cast out at any time? Or he who knows that he was inside and driven outside, did he rather knock, and does he know the door? Also, Ask and you will receive, suits him who knew from whom it was to be asked, from whom also something had been promised, from the God namely of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom the nations did not know any more than any promise of his. And therefore he was speaking to Israel: I was not sent, he says, except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Not yet had he thrown the bread of the children to the dogs, not yet was he commanding to go into the way of the nations. Since indeed at the end he commands that they should go to teach and to baptize the nations, about to receive soon the Holy Spirit, who would lead them into all truth. And this therefore he does for that reason. But if the apostles were destined as teachers for the nations, they themselves also were about to receive as teacher the Holy Spirit, much more was it idle toward us, Seek and you will find, for whom teaching was about to come unbidden through the apostles and to the apostles themselves through the Holy Spirit. All indeed the sayings of the Lord have been set before all; through the ears of the Jews they have passed over to us. But most of them directed at persons have not established for us the property of the admonition, but an example.

choices.why: The legal term 'articulus' means a specific point or article in an argument; 'point' keeps the forensic register without over-translating.
The abstract noun denotes anxious over-scrupulousness; the English cognate preserves the exact nuance of excessive religious anxiety.
The rare noun 'suggillatio' means a bruising or insulting rebuke; 'reproof' captures the corrective tone of the Lord's words to the Jews.
The image is of a tiny drip from a bucket, emphasizing the nations' minimal contact with God; literal rendering keeps the vivid metaphor.
rejected: a drop of water from a bucket

choices.why: The future tense of the verb is preserved to match the rhetorical question's force about the nations who were always outside.
The glossary requires 'the Holy Spirit' for 'paracletus', avoiding the transliteration 'Paraclete'.

pass_b_english: So I come to that point which our own people put forward as an excuse for curiosity, and which heretics press upon us to force scrupulosity upon us. They say, “Seek, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7). Let us remember when the Lord uttered this saying. I think it was at the very first beginnings of his teaching, when everyone was still doubting whether he was the Christ, when Peter had not yet declared him to be the Son of God, and when even John had ceased to be certain about him. Rightly, then, was it said at that time, “Seek, and you will find,” when the one who was not yet known still had to be sought.

And this was as far as the Jews were concerned. For the whole force of that reproof belongs to them, since they had somewhere to seek Christ. “They have,” he says, “Moses and Elijah”—that is, the law and the prophets proclaiming Christ—just as he says openly elsewhere: “Search the Scriptures, in which you hope for salvation; for they speak of me” (John 5:39). This is what “Seek, and you will find” means. For it is clear that what follows also applies to the Jews: “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7). The Jews had formerly been near God; afterwards, cast out for their offenses, they began to be outside God. The Gentiles, however, were never near God—only a drop from a bucket and dust from a threshing floor, and always outside. So how will the one who was always outside knock at a place where he never was? What door does he know, into which he was never received nor ever cast out? Is it not rather the one who knows he was once inside and has been driven out who knocked, and who knows the door?

Likewise, “Ask, and you will receive” (Matthew 7:7) belongs to the one who knew from whom he should ask, and from whom something had been promised—namely, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom the Gentiles knew no more than they knew any of his promises. And that is why he was speaking to Israel: “I was not sent,” he says, “except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). He had not yet thrown the children’s bread to the dogs; he had not yet commanded them to go into the way of the Gentiles. Only at the end did he command them to go and teach and baptize the Gentiles, soon to receive the Holy Spirit, who would lead them into all truth (Matthew 28:19; John 16:13). And this, too, he does for that purpose.

But if the apostles were appointed as teachers for the Gentiles, and they themselves were also about to receive the Holy Spirit as their teacher, then far more, “Seek, and you will find,” was fitting for us, since teaching was about to come to us unsought through the apostles, and to the apostles themselves through the Holy Spirit. All the Lord’s sayings, indeed, are set before all people; through the ears of the Jews they have passed down to us. But most of them were directed at particular persons and have established for us not the force of a command but an example.
